summary: An older MAOI antidepressant used for hard-to-treat depression and sometimes social anxiety. It can work well, but it comes with strict food and medicine interaction rules and real blood pressure risks.
description: Phenelzine (Nardil) is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI). It can be a game-changer for certain types of depression—especially when other antidepressants haven’t worked—but it’s not casual medication. You need a tyramine-restricted diet, careful interaction screening, and close monitoring for blood pressure spikes, mood switching, and suicidality (especially ages 18–24 early in treatment).
patient_summary: Phenelzine (Nardil) is a strong, older antidepressant (MAOI). It can help when other medicines have not worked, but it requires a strict diet and serious attention to drug interactions to prevent dangerous blood pressure reactions. It usually takes weeks to work fully, and you need close monitoring early on for worsening mood, agitation, and suicidal thoughts – especially in younger adults.

primary.context: Approved for depression (major depressive disorder) in adults. Usually used when the options tried first have not worked or caused side effects.

off_label.context: Sometimes used as an alternative option for social anxiety disorder when standard treatments fail or aren’t tolerated.

therapeutic_response.display: Depression: initial effects may be seen in 1–2 weeks, with continued improvement through 4–6 weeks

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dizziness or feeling faint when standing up (a drop in blood pressure)
common_adverse_effects.notes: Feeling dizzy when standing up can happen, especially early or after dose increases. Stand slowly, hydrate, and tell your clinician if you’re fainting or falling.
Sleep can swing either way. If insomnia shows up, dosing timing and sleep structure matter. If hypersomnia shows up, watch daytime functioning and safety.
Some people feel sedated or slowed. This is a big reason to be cautious with driving until you know your baseline.
Feeling unsteady can happen. Add blood pressure drops when standing, and the risk of falls goes up – especially in older adults.
Feeling wound up can happen early or while the dose is being raised. If you feel wired, panicky, or unusually restless, do not push through in silence – call your prescriber.
Changes in orgasm or performance can occur. It’s common enough that it’s worth naming early so adjustments can be made.
Not everyone gains weight, but it can happen. If appetite or weight shifts, track it early rather than discovering it months later.

serious_risks.risk: Hypertensive crisis (sometimes fatal): severe headache, chest pain, palpitations, sweating, nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, dilated pupils; can be triggered by tyramine foods or interacting drugs. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.

Intracranial bleeding reported in association with severe blood pressure increases. MEDICAL EMERGENCY symptoms include sudden neurologic changes, worst headache, weakness, confusion, or vision changes.
Mania/hypomania: mood switching, decreased need for sleep, risky behavior, agitation—especially in bipolar-spectrum illness. Stop-and-reassess urgently with your prescriber.
Seizures: risk increases with predisposition, interactions, or abrupt discontinuation. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Severe discontinuation syndrome with abrupt stopping: agitation, delirium, confusion, hallucinations, myoclonic jerks, seizures, thought disorganization.
Hepatic injury/necrosis and jaundice (rare but serious): dark urine, yellow skin/eyes, severe fatigue, abdominal pain—urgent evaluation needed.
Psychosis/delirium (postmarketing reports): new paranoia, hallucinations, severe confusion—urgent evaluation needed.

safety.black_box_warning: In short-term studies of depression (MDD) and other mental health conditions, antidepressants raised the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior compared with a placebo (dummy pill) in children, teens, and young adults. Anyone thinking about using phenelzine or any other antidepressant for a child, teen, or young adult must weigh this risk against the need for treatment. Short-term studies did not show a higher risk with antidepressants compared with placebo in adults older than 24; the risk went down with antidepressants compared with placebo in adults 65 and older. Depression and some other mental health conditions themselves raise the risk of suicide. People of all ages who start an antidepressant should be watched closely for worsening mood, suicidal thoughts, or unusual changes in behavior. Families and caregivers should watch closely and stay in touch with the health care provider. Phenelzine is not approved for children.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to phenelzine or any component
Abnormal liver function tests or history of hepatic disease
Kidney disease or severe kidney problems
Concurrent use of SSRIs or SNRIs
Taking it at the same time as tricyclic antidepressants and related medicines that strongly affect serotonin or norepinephrine (several medicines in this group must not be combined with it)
Concurrent use of sympathomimetics (including amphetamines, methylphenidate, dopamine, norepinephrine) and related compounds
Concurrent use of local anesthetics containing sympathomimetic vasoconstrictors
Foods high in tyramine (and certain related dietary triggers) during therapy and for 2 weeks after stopping

precautions: Risk of a dangerous blood pressure spike (hypertensive crisis), sometimes fatal: it can happen with foods that contain tyramine, certain supplements, and many interacting medicines. Symptoms can include severe headache (often at the back of the head), a pounding heartbeat, sweating, nausea/vomiting, a stiff neck, sensitivity to light, and chest pain.

Diet is not optional: Aged/fermented/pickled/smoked/spoiled protein foods and certain beverages can trigger dangerous blood pressure spikes. Freshness matters—spoiled or improperly stored protein foods raise risk.
Low blood pressure and fainting: blood pressure can drop when you stand up, especially when the dose is being raised.
CNS depression: Can impair alertness and coordination. Be careful with driving, machinery, and anything where being foggy is dangerous.
Mania/hypomania risk: Antidepressants can trigger mood switching in bipolar disorder. Screen for bipolar symptoms before starting.
Seizure risk: Use caution in people at higher seizure risk or with medications that lower seizure threshold.
Discontinuation syndrome: Abrupt stopping can cause significant neuropsychiatric symptoms; MAOI discontinuation reactions can be more severe and may require conservative tapers.
Not approved for pediatrics: Phenelzine is not FDA-approved for depression in children and is not approved for pediatric use.

interactions.mechanism: High risk of severe reaction due to pharmacodynamic interaction. Washouts are mandatory.
interactions.action: Do not combine. Wait at least 2 weeks after stopping most SSRIs/SNRIs before starting phenelzine. For fluoxetine, wait 5 weeks. After stopping phenelzine, wait 14 days before starting an SSRI/SNRI.

interactions.interactant: Tricyclic antidepressants and related medicines (several in this group must not be combined with it)
interactions.mechanism: High-risk interaction. Can cause severe reactions.
interactions.action: Avoid combination. Use strict washout timing when switching.

interactions.mechanism: Must not be combined; a high-risk interaction.
interactions.action: Avoid combination. Wait at least 14 days between stopping phenelzine and starting bupropion (and vice versa).

interactions.mechanism: Must not be combined; a high-risk interaction.
interactions.action: Avoid combination. Wait at least 14 days between stopping phenelzine and starting buspirone (Canadian labeling notes 10 days).

interactions.mechanism: Dangerous interaction; can be severe and life-threatening.
interactions.action: Do not combine. Make sure all your clinicians (including ER and anesthesia) know you take an MAOI.

interactions.mechanism: Must not be combined; risk of a dangerous interaction.
interactions.action: Avoid. Check OTC cough/cold labels carefully.

interactions.interactant: Sympathomimetics and stimulants (including amphetamines, methylphenidate, dopamine, norepinephrine; and related compounds)
interactions.mechanism: Can raise blood pressure to dangerous levels and trigger a blood pressure crisis.
interactions.action: Avoid. This includes many decongestants and stimulant-type products.

interactions.mechanism: Can worsen CNS depression, coordination impairment, and judgment problems.
interactions.action: Avoid or use extreme caution based on individualized guidance. If you drink at all, discuss explicitly with your prescriber.

interactions.interactant: Tyramine-rich foods and certain dietary triggers (and poor food storage/freshness)
interactions.mechanism: Risk of a dangerous blood pressure spike.
interactions.action: Avoid aged/fermented/pickled/smoked/spoiled protein foods; aged cheeses; certain cured meats; yeast extracts; some alcoholic beverages (beer, wine); and avoid spoiled/improperly stored protein foods. Continue diet restrictions for 2 weeks after stopping.

interactions.interactant: Surgery and anesthesia (general or spinal); local anesthetics with sympathomimetic vasoconstrictors
interactions.mechanism: Unstable blood pressure: it can drop too low or spike too high.
interactions.action: Manufacturer guidance: discontinue phenelzine at least 10 days prior to elective surgery. Any perioperative plan should be coordinated with psychiatry and anesthesia, avoiding meperidine and indirect-acting adrenergic agents.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Blood pressure and heart rate: at the start and regularly while the dose is being raised; watch for both signs of a dangerous blood pressure spike and drops when standing or fainting.
Mental status and safety: worsening depression, suicidality, agitation, unusual behavior changes—especially during the first 1 to 2 months and during dose increases/decreases.
Mood switching: screen for bipolar disorder at baseline; monitor for hypomania/mania (decreased sleep need, increased energy, impulsivity, irritability).
Diet adherence and food safety: ongoing education and reinforcement; freshness and storage of protein foods matter.
Medication reconciliation at every visit: prescription, OTC, supplements, stimulants, cough/cold products—MAOI interactions are the main preventable danger.
Kidney and liver tests: at the start and from time to time when needed; it should not be used with liver problems or severe kidney problems.
Blood sugar if you have diabetes: phenelzine may make insulin work more strongly, so blood sugar is checked closely.
Sleep and daytime functioning: insomnia/hypersomnia, sedation, driving safety, occupational safety.
Discontinuation symptoms if tapering: agitation, delirium, confusion, sleep disruption, myoclonus, seizures—slow taper if symptoms emerge.

special_populations.pregnancy: Animal reproduction studies show harm, and there is little information from human pregnancies. If pregnancy is possible or planned, talk through the risks, benefits and other options. If you take antidepressants while pregnant, you can join the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants (NPRAD) by calling 844-405-6185 (join as early as possible).
special_populations.lactation: It is not known if phenelzine is excreted in breast milk. The decision to continue breastfeeding vs discontinue therapy should weigh infant exposure risk against the benefit of treatment to the mother. If used during breastfeeding, monitor the infant closely for concerning changes and coordinate with pediatrics.
special_populations.pediatric: Not approved for children. Phenelzine is not FDA-approved for depression in children 18 or younger.
special_populations.geriatric: MAOIs can work well in older adults, but the limits are food and medicine interactions and blood pressure effects. The dose is started low and raised slowly, with checks for dizziness when standing, falls, and confusion.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Mild to moderate kidney problems: the label gives no dose change. Severe kidney problems or kidney disease: should not be used.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Should not be used with liver problems, including abnormal liver tests or a history of liver disease.

pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Tyramine- and related dietary exposures can trigger hypertensive crisis; food freshness matters (spoiled/aged/fermented protein foods are higher risk).

dosing.titration: Phenelzine dosing is typically started low and increased gradually based on response and tolerability. Higher doses may be needed for full effect in some patients, but dose increases should be deliberate because blood pressure effects and side effects can intensify during titration.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Stopping phenelzine abruptly can be rough—and MAOIs are associated with more severe discontinuation symptoms in some patients. If you’ve been on it for 4 weeks or longer, tapering is usually the move so you can reduce withdrawal symptoms and also catch relapse early.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Phenelzine (Nardil) is an MAOI antidepressant. In real life, it’s usually a “we’ve tried the usual stuff” medication—effective for some people with major depression who haven’t responded to other antidepressants, and sometimes used as an alternative option for social anxiety. The price of admission is strict interaction screening and a tyramine-restricted diet.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (Unipolar)}: Depression in adults, especially when other antidepressants haven’t worked
{link:condition:social-anxiety-disorder:Social Anxiety Disorder} (off-label): An alternative option when first-line treatments aren’t effective or tolerated

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: It wasn’t instant. One day I realized I’d had a few decent days in a row.
The heaviness started lifting slowly—like the fog backed up a few feet each week.
I didn’t feel ‘high’—I just felt less stuck.
I still got nervous, but I stopped spiraling before I even spoke.
Social situations felt less like a threat and more like… just a thing.
My body stopped reacting like everything was an emergency.

items.category: Side effects that can be annoying
quotes: Standing up too fast made me feel lightheaded.
I was tired in a weird way—like my energy didn’t match my mind.
My sleep got strange at first: either too much or not enough.
items.note: Blood pressure changes (especially orthostatic symptoms) and sleep changes can happen, particularly during dose changes.

quotes: The diet rules felt intimidating until I got used to it.
I had to check every cold medicine label like my life depended on it.
I learned fast that ‘just one’ interaction can be a big deal.
items.note: This is the defining feature of phenelzine: it can work well, but you must take the interaction rules seriously.

sections.intro: Everyone’s different, but phenelzine tends to have a pretty recognizable “feel” once it starts working—and it also has some very specific downsides.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Phenelzine isn’t a quick-hit medication. Even though it’s absorbed fast, the clinical antidepressant effect usually builds over weeks.
key_points: Within an hour: Drug levels peak quickly (time to peak around 43 minutes)
1–2 weeks: Some people notice early mood/anxiety changes
4–6 weeks: A more complete antidepressant response often becomes clearer
After stopping: Interaction risk can persist for about 2 weeks, which is why washout periods matter

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Phenelzine can be highly effective for the right patient, especially when other antidepressants haven’t helped. But it’s not a casual first-line choice because the risks are mostly about prevention: hypertensive crisis, dangerous interactions, and mood switching. The best outcomes happen when dosing is gradual, the diet is consistent, and the prescriber/patient treat interactions like a non-negotiable.
sections.metric: Symptom improvement in depression and/or social anxiety over weeks
sections.clinical_details: Clinically, response is usually judged by real-world function: less depressive shutdown, improved motivation, better sleep stability, reduced anxiety intensity, and fewer day-to-day crashes. For social anxiety, improvement often shows up as reduced anticipatory dread and fewer physical panic-like reactions in social settings. Because MAOI effects and interaction risk persist after discontinuation, planning (washouts, medication changes, and surgery/anesthesia) is part of efficacy and safety.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: This medication has strict interaction rules. The big emergencies are hypertensive crisis and dangerous drug combinations.
sections.black_box: In short-term studies of depression (MDD) and other mental health conditions, antidepressants raised the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior compared with a placebo (dummy pill) in children, teens, and young adults. Anyone thinking about using phenelzine or any other antidepressant for a child, teen, or young adult must weigh this risk against the need for treatment. Short-term studies did not show a higher risk with antidepressants compared with placebo in adults older than 24; the risk went down with antidepressants compared with placebo in adults 65 and older. Depression and some other mental health conditions themselves raise the risk of suicide. People of all ages who start an antidepressant should be watched closely for worsening mood, suicidal thoughts, or unusual changes in behavior. Families and caregivers should watch closely and stay in touch with the health care provider. Phenelzine is not approved for children.
other: Hypertensive crisis risk (sometimes fatal): Can happen with tyramine-containing foods, certain supplements, and many interacting medications. Symptoms can include severe headache (often occipital), palpitations, sweating, nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, and chest pain.

Diet is not optional: Aged/fermented/pickled/smoked/spoiled protein foods and certain beverages can trigger dangerous blood pressure spikes. Freshness matters—spoiled or improperly stored protein foods raise risk.
Hypotension and fainting: Postural (orthostatic) hypotension can occur, especially during dose increases.
CNS depression: Can impair alertness and coordination. Be careful with driving, machinery, and anything where being foggy is dangerous.
Mania/hypomania risk: Antidepressants can trigger mood switching in bipolar disorder. Screen for bipolar symptoms before starting.
Seizure risk: Use caution in people at higher seizure risk or with medications that lower seizure threshold.
Discontinuation syndrome: Abrupt stopping can cause significant neuropsychiatric symptoms; MAOI discontinuation reactions can be more severe and may require conservative tapers.
Not approved for pediatrics: Phenelzine is not FDA-approved for depression in children and is not approved for pediatric use.
patient_counseling: Know the red-flag emergency symptoms: sudden severe headache, chest pain, palpitations, sweating, vomiting, stiff neck, or vision changes—get emergency care.
Follow the tyramine-restricted diet the whole time you’re on it and for 2 weeks after stopping.
Before you take any new medication (including cough/cold meds, supplements, stimulants, or weight-loss products), check with your prescriber/pharmacist. MAOI interactions can be dangerous.
Early treatment and dose changes are the highest-risk windows for mood worsening, agitation, insomnia, impulsivity, and suicidal thoughts—tell someone and tell your clinician if you notice changes.
If you have any history of bipolar symptoms (periods of decreased sleep, increased energy, racing thoughts, risky behavior), say that upfront before starting.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Common themes: blood pressure changes (especially standing dizziness), sleep disturbance, fatigue, and nervous system effects like jitteriness or sedation. Serious risks include hypertensive crisis (from interactions/diet) and mood switching.

sections.intro: Phenelzine has some of the strictest interaction rules in psychiatry. Many combinations are flat-out contraindicated because they can trigger hypertensive crisis, serotonin toxicity-like reactions, severe blood pressure instability, or dangerous CNS effects.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Stopping phenelzine abruptly can be rough—and MAOIs are associated with more severe discontinuation symptoms in some patients. If you’ve been on it for 4 weeks or longer, tapering is usually the move so you can reduce withdrawal symptoms and also catch relapse early.
key_points: If treatment lasted ≥4 weeks: taper gradually (example range: over 2–4 weeks).
If treatment lasted ~2–3 weeks: taper may be done over 1–2 weeks.
If treatment lasted <2 weeks: tapering often isn’t necessary, but individual factors still matter.
Reasons to taper slower (sometimes ≥4 weeks or longer): high doses, prior discontinuation symptoms, longer treatment duration, or significant anxiety/activation during dose changes.
If withdrawal symptoms are intolerable: return to the previously tolerated dose and taper more slowly.
Some long-term patients (e.g., >6 months) with a history of discontinuation syndrome may benefit from a much longer taper (sometimes >3 months).
Because MAOI effects and interaction risk can persist after stopping, medication switches require planned washouts even while tapering.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Phenelzine dosing is typically started low and increased gradually based on response and tolerability. Higher doses may be needed for full effect in some patients, but dose increases should be deliberate because blood pressure effects and side effects can intensify during titration.

adult.mdd_initial: 15 mg PO once to three times daily
adult.mdd_titration: Increase in 15 mg/day increments at intervals of at least 2 to 4 days based on response and tolerability (some experts titrate more slowly, e.g., every 2 to 3 weeks)
adult.mdd_typical: Up to 60 mg/day in 3 divided doses
adult.mdd_max: Some people may need up to 90 mg/day for the best response
adult.social_anxiety_protocol: Off-label: 15 mg PO once daily for 3 days, then 30 mg once daily for 4 days; start of week 2 increase to 45 mg once daily; start of week 3 increase to 60 mg/day (if ≥60 mg/day, divide into 2 equal daily doses). Doses up to 90 mg/day have been studied.
adult.older_adult: Use caution and start at the low end; some clinicians start 7.5 mg/day and increase by 7.5 mg/day every 4 to 8 days as tolerated to a usual range of 22.5 to 60 mg/day
adult.renal_impairment: Mild to moderate impairment: no adjustment provided in labeling. Severe renal impairment: contraindicated.

sections.simple_explanation: Phenelzine is dosed gradually because the therapeutic benefit builds over weeks, and side effects (especially blood pressure changes) often show up during dose increases. If your daily dose gets to 60 mg or higher, it’s commonly split into two doses to improve tolerability.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Phenelzine can be used in adults, but special populations require extra caution. The biggest limiting factors are interaction risk, blood pressure effects, and limited data in pregnancy/lactation.
sections.pregnancy: Animal reproduction studies show adverse events, and human pregnancy data are limited. If pregnancy is possible or planned, discuss risks/benefits and alternatives. Pregnant patients exposed to antidepressants can enroll in the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants (NPRAD) by calling 844-405-6185 (enroll as early as possible).
sections.lactation: It is not known if phenelzine is excreted in breast milk. The decision to continue breastfeeding vs discontinue therapy should weigh infant exposure risk against the benefit of treatment to the mother. If used during breastfeeding, monitor the infant closely for concerning changes and coordinate with pediatrics.
sections.pediatrics: Not approved for children. Phenelzine is not FDA-approved for depression in children 18 or younger.
sections.geriatrics: MAOIs can be effective in older adults, but the limiting factors are diet/drug interactions and blood pressure effects. Start low, titrate slowly, and monitor orthostasis, falls, and confusion risk.
sections.hepatic: Contraindicated, including abnormal liver function tests or history of hepatic disease.
sections.renal: Mild to moderate impairment: no adjustment provided in labeling. Severe renal impairment/renal disease: contraindicated.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Phenelzine is straightforward in formulation—most of the complexity is the interaction and diet management, not the dosage form.
items: Oral tablet: 15 mg (brand Nardil and generic phenelzine sulfate)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Phenelzine inhibits monoamine oxidase (MAO), an enzyme that breaks down key neurotransmitters. By blocking MAO, phenelzine increases the availability of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine in the brain. That broad monoamine boost is part of why it can work when other antidepressants fail—and also why the interaction list is intense.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Phenelzine is usually not a first-line antidepressant. It’s more of a specialist tool: useful for treatment-resistant depression or specific symptom patterns where MAOIs can shine, and as an alternative option for social anxiety when standard therapies haven’t worked. The practical reality is that success depends as much on education, diet consistency, and interaction screening as it does on the dose.

faqs.a: Phenelzine is an MAOI antidepressant used for unipolar major depressive disorder in adults. In practice, it’s often used when other antidepressants haven’t worked. It’s also sometimes used off-label as an alternative option for social anxiety disorder.

faqs.q: How long does phenelzine take to work?
faqs.a: Even though it’s absorbed quickly, the clinical effect usually builds over weeks. Some people notice changes in 1–2 weeks, with continued improvement through about 4–6 weeks.

faqs.q: Why does phenelzine have food restrictions?
faqs.a: Because it is an MAOI. Certain foods high in tyramine (especially aged, fermented, pickled, cured, or spoiled protein foods) can trigger a dangerous blood pressure spike (hypertensive crisis). How fresh food is and how it is stored matter – not just the ingredient list.

faqs.q: How long do I need to follow the MAOI diet after stopping phenelzine?
faqs.a: Continue the dietary restrictions for 2 weeks after stopping phenelzine. The medication’s interaction risk can persist even after the last dose.

faqs.q: What are the most dangerous drug interactions with phenelzine?
faqs.a: The high-risk category includes SSRIs/SNRIs, many tricyclics and related agents, bupropion, buspirone, meperidine, dextromethorphan, stimulants/sympathomimetics (including many decongestants), and certain anesthesia-related drugs. Always check before adding anything new, including OTC cold meds and supplements.

faqs.q: What washout time is needed when switching antidepressants?
faqs.a: In general, wait 14 days between stopping phenelzine and starting most other antidepressants (and vice versa). For fluoxetine, wait 5 weeks before starting phenelzine because its metabolites last longer. These washouts exist to prevent dangerous interactions.

Antidepressants carry a boxed warning about increased risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults (18–24) in short-term studies. That doesn’t mean it will happen, but it means early monitoring is essential—especially in the first 1–2 months and during dose changes.

Yes, antidepressants can trigger mania or hypomania in people with bipolar disorder. That’s why screening for bipolar symptoms matters before starting, and why new signs like decreased sleep need, increased energy, irritability, or risky behavior should be reported immediately.

faqs.q: What are the signs of a dangerous blood pressure spike (hypertensive crisis)?
faqs.a: Red flags include sudden severe headache (often in the back of the head), palpitations, sweating, nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness, sensitivity to light, chest pain, or feeling acutely unwell. This is an emergency—seek immediate medical care.

faqs.q: How do you taper off phenelzine safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it for 4 weeks or more, tapering over about 2–4 weeks is commonly used to reduce withdrawal symptoms and to watch for relapse. Some people need slower tapers—especially at higher doses, longer treatment duration, or if they’ve had discontinuation symptoms before. If withdrawal becomes intolerable, the typical move is to return to the last tolerated dose and taper more gradually.

faqs.q: Is phenelzine approved for kids or teens?

seo.description: Phenelzine (Nardil) is an MAOI for depression and sometimes social anxiety. Learn dosing, how long it takes to work, major side effects, strict food rules (tyramine diet), dangerous drug interactions, and safe tapering.
